title.zh: 卡科爾托克首領翁戈爾托克

region.zh: 南格陵蘭卡科爾托克（尤利安娜霍布一帶）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; West Greenland tradition of the ancient Scandinavian settlers, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 54 (1) 'Ungortok, the Chief of Kakortok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: The only trace of the ancient Scandinavian settlers: taunted into killing a shell-gathering Kavdlunak, the kayaker kills a second and the Kavdlunait revenge themselves with axes, sparing only two brothers — the younger losing an arm before Kaisape's eyes ('As long as thou livest thou won't surely forget thy poor brother'). Years on, Kaisape builds a false iceberg of white seal-skins in a hollowed spar, drifts it up to Kakortok, fires the house with juniper fagots, and hunts Ungortok with a barren woman's boot-shelf arrow charmed by an Eastlander — through the sleeping wife's throat, past the thin-as-a-shadow dodge, until the charmed shaft goes through the protruding chin.
summary.zh: 關於古斯堪地那維亞移民的唯一口傳：皮艇客被戲弄著射殺撿貝的卡夫德盧納克，再殺第二人——仇家提斧屠村，兄弟二人僅以身免，幼弟斷臂，兄長卡伊薩佩銘記於心。多年後他以白海豹皮裝入掏空浮木，偽裝冰山漂至卡科爾托克，以杜松柴火焚其屋；再向東地人求得『不孕婦靴架之木』所製的神箭——穿過熟睡妻子的咽喉、避過扁如薄影的閃避，最終穿透首領昂出的下巴，報了斷臂之仇。

sensitivity.note: Rink: the only trace of intelligence concerning the ancient Scandinavian settlers found in the country; Kakortok = Julianehaab with Scandinavian ruins 8 miles distant. Graphic mutilation and killing recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: It once happened that a kayaker from Arpatsivik came rowing up the firth, trying his new bird-javelin as he went along. On approaching Kakortok, where the first Kavdlunait had taken up their abode, he saw one of them gathering shells on the beach, and presently he called out to him, 'Let us see whether thou canst hit me with thy lance.' The kayaker would not comply, although the other continued asking him; at last, however, the master of the place, named Ungortok, made his appearance, and said, 'Since he seems so very anxious about it, take good aim at him' — and soon the kayaker sent out his spear in good earnest, and killed him on the spot. Ungortok, however, did not reproach him, but only said, 'It certainly is no fault of thine, since thou hast only done as thou wast bidden.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (1) 'Ungortok, the Chief of Kakortok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When winter came it was a general belief that the Kavdlunait would come and avenge the death of their countryman; but summer came round again, and even two summers passed quickly by. At the beginning of the third winter the same kayaker again rowed up to Kakortok, provided with the usual hunting tools, bladder and all. This time he again happened to see a Kavdlunak gathering shells, and somehow took a fancy to kill him too: rowing up on the sunlit side of the water, launching his spear, he killed him at once, returned home unobserved, and told how he had done away with one of the Kavdlunait. They reproached him with not having let their chief know of this — 'The first time I only killed him because I was asked over and over again to do so.' Some time after, a girl sent out to draw water in the evening noticed the reflection of something red down in the water; turning round she was horrified at seeing a great crowd of Kavdlunait — so confounded that she left the pail behind and hurried into the house. The enemies posted themselves in front of the door and the windows; one of the inmates ran out but was soon killed with an axe and cast aside — they were all despatched in this way, only two brothers remaining unhurt, who happily escaped out on the ice.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (1) 'Ungortok, the Chief of Kakortok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Kavdlunait soon caught sight of them: 'Those are the last of the lot; let us be after them' — and at once began the pursuit, their leader claiming to be the quickest. The brothers' speed was greatly retarded, the younger having new soles to his boots which made them slippery and often cost him his footing. They reached the opposite shore; Kaisape, the elder, succeeded in climbing the icy beach, but the younger fell and was quickly overtaken. Ungortok cut off his left arm, and held it up before his brother, saying, 'Kaisape! as long as thou livest thou won't surely forget thy poor brother.' Kaisape, unarmed, could render him no assistance, but quickly took to his heels, crossing the country for Kangermiutsiak where his father-in-law was living. He remained there all winter, was presented with a kayak, kayaked south in summer to learn some magic lay that had power to charm his enemies, wintered again, and went north to find himself a companion — at every place inquiring first if there happened to be a couple of brothers, then examining the inside fur of their boots to see whether they had any lice in them, travelling far and wide before he found two brothers of whom the younger was altogether without lice. This one he persuaded to assist him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (1) 'Ungortok, the Chief of Kakortok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Very intent on catching seals, of all he caught he had the hairs removed from the skins to be used for white skins; then he found a large piece of driftwood, excavated it with his knife until it was all hollow like a tube, made a cover to fit tightly at one end, furnished both sides with little holes and stoppers of wood. He put all the white skins inside the hollow space, shut it up, put it down into the water, and all the kayakers joined in towing it down the inlet to Pingiviarnek, where, having got out the skins and attached strings, they hoisted and spread them like sails, so that the boat came to have the appearance of a somewhat dirty iceberg. The people got in, the boat was pushed off, Kaisape gave the order 'Let the skins be spread!' — and the people on shore were astonished to see how very like it was to an iceberg floating slowly along. When the fair wind set in, the firth filled with broken bits of ice; several boats followed in his wake, their crews landing a little north of Kakortok to gather fagots of juniper, while Kaisape and his helpmates, well hidden in the hollow wood and keeping a constant look-out through the peep-holes, drifted straight on towards the house. Once they distinctly heard it announced, 'The Kaladlit are coming!' — all came running out, but when the master had reassured them, 'It is nothing but ice,' they again retired, and Kaisape said, 'Now, quick! they won't be coming out for a while, I think.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (1) 'Ungortok, the Chief of Kakortok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: They got out on shore, and, well loaded with juniper fagots, surrounded the house; Kaisape filled up the doorway with fuel and stuck fire to it, so that all the people inside were burned, and those who tried to escape through the passage were also consumed. But Kaisape cared little for the people in general; his thoughts all centred in Ungortok — 'Kaisape! the man whom thou seekest is up there.' The chief had left the burning house through a window and was flying with his little son in his arms; at the lake the father threw his child into the water that it might rather die unwounded, and Kaisape, not being able to overtake his antagonist, was forced to return to his crew. Ungortok ran on till he reached Igaliko, and established himself with another chief named Olave; on finding that Kaisape would not leave him at peace he removed to the head of the firth Agdluitsok, settling at Sioralik, while Kaisape established himself at the outlet of the same firth. The following summer he again left in pursuit, Ungortok getting to the coast opposite the island of Aluk, Kaisape tracing him to the north side of the same island, where he took up his abode; there he consulted the Eastlanders with regard to some means of killing Ungortok, and at last one stood forth: 'I will get thee a bit of wood from a barren woman's boot-shelf, out of which thou must shape thine arrow' — having pronounced some spell upon it, he handed it over, and Kaisape acknowledged the gift: 'If it comes true that this shall help me, I will be bound to give thee my aid in hunting and fishing.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (1) 'Ungortok, the Chief of Kakortok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He made as many arrows as could be contained in a sealskin quiver, adding last of all the precious charmed one, and with his helpmates left for the great lake in front of Ungortok's house, sticking all the arrows in the ground at a certain distance from each other, and finally the charmed one. Letting his companion remain below by the lake, he cautiously mounted high hills, from whence he could see Ungortok striding to and fro outside his house, talking to himself and mentioning the name of Kaisape. In the dusk he stole away to the house and looked in at the window, holding his bow ready bent; Ungortok was passing up and down as swiftly as a shadow, making a sure aim impossible — so Kaisape levelled his bow at Ungortok's wife, who lay sleeping with a baby at her breast; hearing a noise, Ungortok gave a look at his wife and perceived the arrow sticking fast in her throat. Kaisape ran back to the lake to fetch another arrow while Ungortok sped after him with the uplifted axe that had formerly killed his brother; the second arrow was escaped by falling down and making himself so thin that nothing but his chin remained visible, and before long Kaisape had spent all his arrows without having hit his mark — Ungortok broke them in twain and threw them into the lake. But at last Kaisape caught hold of the charmed arrow, and this went straight through the protruding chin down into the throat. As Ungortok did not expire immediately, Kaisape took flight, shortly followed by the wounded Ungortok; running a good long while, he suddenly felt his throat getting dry and fell down totally exhausted — remembering Ungortok, he rose again and ran back to find his dead body lying close by. He cut off his right arm and held it up before the dead man, repeating his own words, 'Behold this arm, which thou wilt surely never forget!' He also killed the orphan child, and taking the old Eastlander with him, travelled back to Kangermiutsiak, where he sustained the old man, whose bones, according to report, were laid to rest in that same place.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (1) 'Ungortok, the Chief of Kakortok'; not verbatim.

title.en: The First Meeting of the Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait
title.zh: 格陵蘭人與古卡夫德盧納人的初遇

region.zh: 努克地區康格蘇內克與射箭山

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; Godthaab narrators, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 54 (2) 'The First Meeting of the Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait in Greenland', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A boat's crew landing at Nook finds the fiord already settled by the first Kavdlunak settlers, who treat them kindly — but they hasten away afraid, returning with many boats until the two peoples learn each other's language. At Kapisilik a Kavdlunak and a Kalalek become inseparable friends, first-rate archers whose arrows always fall side by side — until the wager 'he who fails shall be thrown down the precipice' is accepted against the Greenlander's protest, the Kavdlunak misses, the Kalalek pierces the skin target in the centre, and the mountain has been called Pisigsarfik (the shooting-place) ever since.
summary.zh: 一支大舟在努克登岸，發現峽灣裡早住著第一批卡夫德盧納克移民；對方以禮相待，格陵蘭人卻驚懼而去——直至眾舟齊至、兩族互學語言。在卡皮西利克，一名卡夫德盧納克與一名格陵蘭人結成莫逆，箭術相當、箭箭並落——直到前者執意立誓：『射不中者墜崖而死。』格陵蘭人勸阻無效；卡夫德盧納克脫靶，格陵蘭人正中皮靶，前者依願墜崖，族人只道他自取其禍。此山自此名為皮西格薩爾菲克——射箭之地。

sensitivity.note: Rink's note: compiled from six manuscripts, localised for the Julianehaab (Easterbygd) and Godthaab (Westerbygd) districts; linked to tale 18 (Navaranak) to explain the beginning of the warfare. Suicide by wager recorded as told.

passages.text: In former times, when the coast was less peopled than now, a boat's crew landed at Nook (Godthaab); they found no people, and traversed the fiord to Kangersunek. Half-way up to the east of Kornok, near Ivangiusak, they came upon a large house; but on getting closer to it they did not know what to make of the people, seeing that they were not Kaladlit — in this manner they had quite unexpectedly come across the first Kavdlunak settlers. These likewise for the first time saw the natives of the country, and treated them kindly and civilly; but the Greenlanders nevertheless feared them, and made for their boats. On getting farther up the fiord they found many Kavdlunait stationed; however, they did not put in anywhere, but hastened away as fast as possible. When the boat and its crew returned from their summer trip in the fiord, they told their countrymen all around of their encounter with the foreigners, and many of them now travelled up to see them. Many boats having thus reached Kangersunek, they now began to have intercourse with the Kavdlunait, seeing that they were well disposed towards them; later on in the summer many more Kaladlit arrived, and the foreigners began to learn their language.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (2) 'The First Meeting of the Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait in Greenland'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At Kapisilik a Kavdlunak and a Kalalek, it is said, became such fast friends that they would not be separated, but were constantly together; they tried to excel each other at different games and feats of dexterity, and their countrymen on both sides were greatly diverted as lookers-on — but being both first-rate archers, their arrows always fell side by side. One day the Kavdlunak said, 'Come, let us climb yon lofty hill; but first we will stretch a skin for a target to aim at on that little islet yonder; then we will try which of us can hit the mark. He who fails shall be thrown down the precipice, and the other remain the conqueror.' 'No, I will not agree to that, because we are friends, and none of us shall perish' — but the Kavdlunak persisted so long that his own countrymen at last said, 'Well, let him be thrown down as it is at his own will,' and the Kalalek at last gave in, and they climbed the mountain together, accompanied by a crowd of spectators. The Kavdlunak was the first to shoot, but altogether failed; then the Kalalek came in for his turn, and pierced the skin in the centre. According to his own desire the Kavdlunak was hurled down the precipice, and his countrymen only thought it served him right for having thus recklessly pledged his life. From that day until the present this mountain has been called Pisigsarfik (the shooting-place).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (2) 'The First Meeting of the Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait in Greenland'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Ancient Kavdlunait's Ruin Near Arsut

region.en: Iminguit bay and Ikat, near Arsut, South Greenland
region.zh: 南格陵蘭阿爾舒特附近的伊明圭特灣與伊卡特

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; common tradition at Arsut, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 54 (3) 'The Ancient Kavdlunait's Ruin near Arsut', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A kayaker striking the sides of a Kavdlunait tent at Iminguit silences their jesting — peeping in, he finds them all dead with fear. At Ikat the Kavdlunait taken by surprise flee with their children upon thin ice and are drowned — it is said only a few years ago they might be seen at the bottom of the sea; and the common tradition at Arsut holds that whenever they become visible it is a sure foreboding that one of the people will die.
summary.zh: 一名皮艇客在伊明圭特灣敲擊卡夫德盧納克的帳篷，戲語漸息——窺看之下，他們竟全數嚇死。伊卡特處的移民攜子逃上薄冰，破冰溺斃——據說數年前還能在海底看見他們；阿爾舒特當地相傳：這些身影一旦顯現，便是村中有人將死的預兆。

sensitivity.note: Place-legend attached to actual Scandinavian ruins; drowning recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: A kayaker one day went to the bay of Iminguit to catch thong-seals. Arriving there he observed a tent belonging to some Kavdlunait. He heard them jesting and prating inside, and was strongly minded to go and look in upon them; accordingly he left his kayak, went up to the place, and began to strike on the sides of the tent. This made them apprehensive, and they now became quiet, which only encouraged him to continue all the more, until he succeeded in silencing them altogether. Then he took a peep in at them, and behold! they were all dead with fear.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (3) 'The Ancient Kavdlunait's Ruin near Arsut'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At Ikat the Kavdlunait living there were also taken by surprise by the Kaladlit, and four fathers fled with their children out upon the ice, which, however, being too thin, broke through with them, so that all were drowned — and it is said that only a few years ago they might be seen at the bottom of the sea. It is a common tradition at Arsut that whenever they become visible it is a sure foreboding that one of the people will die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (3) 'The Ancient Kavdlunait's Ruin near Arsut'; not verbatim.

title.en: Encounter of Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait on the Ice

region.en: Frozen lake of the south country, North Greenland telling
region.zh: 南方凍湖（北格陵蘭講述本）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; tale received from North Greenland, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 54 (4) 'Encounter of Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait on the Ice', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Attacked in autumn when the lakes are frozen, a house is put to the axe while the newly delivered housewife is sorceried through a window; a mother is dragged across the frozen lake by a rope tied to her tuft of hair. Hidden among stone-heaps, the enraged son sends two girls out on the ice as bait — the slippery Kavdlunait fall on their backs, sideways, tottering — and with spear and spare spear he despatches the whole enemy before the girls reach the open sea, then pierces them through their bellies to complete his vengeance.
summary.zh: 秋日湖凍之際，仇家提斧攻屋；產婦被巫術送出窗外，老母被繩縛髮髻拖過凍湖。藏於石堆的兒子怒極，遣兩名少女上冰為餌——卡夫德盧納克人在冰上連連跌倒；他執叉攜備叉衝上冰面，未等少女抵達海面便殺盡來敵，又逐一刺穿其腹，以完復仇——歸屋所見，盡是同袍屍骸。

sensitivity.note: Graphic massacre and dragging of the mother recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: It is said that the Kaladlit of the south country at times were attacked in the autumn season, when the lakes were frozen over, and the sea-shore was all bordered with ice. It once happened that a man had been out hunting, and came home with two white whales; in the evening a couple of girls came running into the house crying, 'The enemy is coming upon us!' At which the man got into a passion, and tore the fishing-line which he was busily winding up; but when he was about to go out, the Kavdlunait were already making an onset upon the house. The housewife, who had been newly delivered of a child, was by means of sorcery got through a window, and several escaped the same way; but all those who attempted to get through the entrance were miserably killed. The master of the house, who had escaped along with his wife, returned to bring his mother out, but finding her badly wounded had to leave her to her fate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (4) 'Encounter of Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait on the Ice'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Some had in this manner escaped and hastened away to hide themselves among the stone-heaps, from whence they heard the enemy's wild shouts of triumph; the man had to witness his mother being dragged across the frozen lake by a rope fastened to her tuft of hair. Though greatly enraged he tried to keep quiet in his hiding-place, but ordered the two girls down on the ice: 'Now ye go on to the edge of the water, and when they overtake you plunge yourselves into the sea.' Sobbing and crying they did as they were bid; no sooner had they been observed by the Kavdlunait than they were seen to run out after them — but the ice was too slippery for them, and they lost their footing, some falling on their backs, others sideways, and some going tottering about. The angry Kalalek now asked his people how many of the enemy had gone out on the ice and whether any of them were still on shore; they did not agree about this, but at last one said that all of them had now got down. Immediately the furious Kalalek rushed out on the ice, spear in hand, and another one in store: the first of the Kavdlunait he met was instantly speared; the others fell on approaching him, and were likewise killed. When the point of his spear had got too sticky with blood he would only take time to blow it away; and before the girls had reached the open sea he had despatched the whole of them. However, he turned back again, and pierced them through their bellies in order to complete his vengeance, and then returned to the house, where he found the inmates all killed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 54 (4) 'Encounter of Kaladlit with the Ancient Kavdlunait on the Ice'; not verbatim.

title.en: Pisagsak and the Kivigtok: The Ladder of the Cliff
title.zh: 皮薩克薩克與奇維托克：崖上的長梯

region.en: Steep mountain-wall with a suspended ladder, inland plain
region.zh: 懸梯高崖與內陸棉草平原

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; received from one narrator, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 55 'Pisagsak and the Kivigtok', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Carried by his sport to a mountain-wall hung with a long ladder, Pisagsak is claimed by a shivering old kivigtok — 'I would like thee for my companion' — and learns the hidden plain: boots on the cross-bar, reindeer from the pot, wife-stealing at the Kavdlunait's water-spring (his own catch deliberately a wrinkled old woman who stays gladly), until the day the Kavdlunait assault from the sea-side: the ladder is loosened at the top, a tremendous cry, and the Kavdlunait are all swallowed up by the sea, not one escaping. The old woman dies of sheer old age, Pisagsak goes home with the kivigtok's warning, and never afterwards leaves home.
summary.zh: 逐獵忘返的皮薩克薩克來到一道垂著長梯的絕壁下，被一個瑟縮的老奇維托克收留——『我要你做我的伴』——習得隱谷生活：橫樑上的靴串、鍋中燉鹿、以及在卡夫德盧納人泉邊搶親（他自己故意搶回一位皺紋滿面的老嫗，老嫗卻樂意留下）。仇家自海面來犯之日，老者於崖頂鬆開梯索——一聲慘叫，卡夫德盧納人盡葬海中。老嫗壽終，皮薩克薩克攔下老者的口信回到族人之中，此後再未離家。

sensitivity.note: Rink notes the tale doubtful for inclusion among the Kavdlunait stories. Drowning of the assault party recorded as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Pisagsak one day went out kayaking in order to try his new bird-javelin, and in the excitement of the sport was carried far away from his homestead; at length he arrived at the foot of a steep mountain-wall, from the top of which a long ladder was suspended, and having reached the top with great trouble surveyed a little plain spreading below on the other side, covered with cotton-grass, the down carried along by the wind. The plain was bordered by another mountain-wall, which he climbed likewise, and far below on the other side beheld a little house; stealing along to it he peeped in at the window, but only saw one old kivigtok sitting at his work. When he was about to withdraw as noiselessly as he had come, the old man accosted him: 'Of course I have seen thee, so please to come inside' — all shaky and shivering, in a peevish voice, 'I would like thee for my companion; thou hadst better stop with me.' He went out and returned with some dried meat and tallow; Pisagsak satisfied his hunger, and his host then took some boiled reindeer out of a large pot, which pleased him even more. At night Pisagsak could hardly sleep for fear of his aged housemate; in the morning the old man had gone off, and on looking round he perceived a great number of boots dangling on the cross-bar beneath the roof — he took them, overhauled them, put them up to dry, and proceeded to do the cooking.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 55 'Pisagsak and the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the evening he heard a noise, and soon saw the old man coming along with two large bucks: 'Here is some work for thee to put thy hand to; come away and skin them at once.' Pisagsak remained with him and took charge of the household work; he learned to snare partridges and shoot reindeer, and after some time grew very dexterous as a sportsman. One evening the old kivigtok went on, saying, 'To-morrow is the day when the women of the Kavdlunait use to come here to fetch water. I dare-say there will be some young girls among them: we will go and have a look at them.' They arrived at a place from whence they could see a great many houses, beyond which a spring was visible, and hid themselves behind some large stones; about sunrise the first girl came, filled her pail, and retired, others following, some handsome, some old and slow. A young and very beautiful woman approached, had just put down her pail and commenced pouring in water, when Pisagsak noticed that the old man was getting very excited and trembled all over — the next moment he sprang on the young girl and carried her away, having first stuffed her mouth to keep her from calling out; Pisagsak of course followed them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 55 'Pisagsak and the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Having reached their house, they took away her boots to prevent her from running away, and only went out to hunt by turns in order to keep watch on her; however, the girl at length got reconciled to her fate and gave up all idea of flight, and they could now venture to leave the house together — on their return they always found the work of the house ready done, and their clothes and boots mended. Another day Pisagsak again accompanied the old man to the spring to look at the girls; this time the old man ordered Pisagsak to catch a nice one, but he lingered and waited till an old woman, wrinkled all over, made her appearance, then rushed on and took hold of her and brought her home — and when the old woman had passed one day with them she came to like them, and did not care to go back. Now they had two women in the house, and they did exceedingly well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 55 'Pisagsak and the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the kivigtok said to Pisagsak, 'To-morrow the Kavdlunait will be making an assault on us from the sea-side; let us go and look out for them.' They went away to the top of the high cliff where the ladder was made fast, and saw several boats approaching the coast: 'Now they begin to land; but when they have all got on shore and try to climb the ladder, I will loosen it on the top, and then thou wilt see a sight.' Pisagsak stood in great expectation; presently they had all got on the ladder, but not until the first of them appeared wielding his lance above the summit of the steep mountain-side did the kivigtok loosen the cords from the stone — a tremendous cry now followed, and the Kavdlunait were all swallowed up by the sea; not one escaped. After this catastrophe the others for some time lived on in their usual way, but the old woman at length took ill and died from sheer old age, and after that Pisagsak began to long for his own home. When he told his master he did not object, but remarked, 'Tell the Kavdlunait yonder that they had better not attack me; if they do, I shall certainly destroy them.' Pisagsak now returned to his relatives, who had totally given him up, brought them the message of the kivigtok, and never afterwards left home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 55 'Pisagsak and the Kivigtok'; not verbatim.
